text: You now have the Journal Entries Report, Account Analysis Report, and Open Account Balances Listing in your toolkit. This lesson puts them to work in the activity they most directly support: proving a subledger's records agree with what landed in the General Ledger.

Even with a well-tested SLA configuration, companies still reconcile subledger to GL as a recurring control, typically at month-end. Payables maintains its own record of what's owed to suppliers. GL separately holds a balance on AP Trade, built from transferred journal entries. These should always agree - but that's worth proving, not assuming.

At its core, reconciliation compares two numbers: the subledger's own balance for a control account, against the GL balance on the corresponding account, for the same ledger and period. If they match, the account is considered in balance for that period.

When they don't match, the difference usually traces to one of a few causes: a subledger entry created but never transferred, a manual journal posted directly to the GL control account outside SLA entirely, or a timing difference between when something was accounted and when it transferred.

In practice, reconciliation starts with the two headline numbers. If they disagree, move to the Account Analysis Report to see everything that posted to the GL control account for the period, cross-referenced against the subledger's own open-items detail, to isolate exactly which item is causing the gap.

So remember: reconciliation compares subledger balance to GL balance, and differences usually mean a missed transfer, a bypassing manual journal, or a timing gap.
